CLEAR: Capability-Aware Latent Ordering for
Adaptive Interaction with Movable Objects
Anonymous Authors
Abstract— Planning physical interactions in cluttered envi-
ronments requires reasoning about robot capabilities. For exam-
ple, a legged robot may climb stairs, while a wheeled robot may
need an alternative route. However, the ability to move objects
does not ensure task completion, as the interaction order and
resulting object configurations can block subsequent actions. To
address this challenge, we propose a capability-aware planner
that jointly determines which objects to interact with, in which
order, and how to move them. Our planner, Capability-Aware
Latent Ordering for Adaptive Interaction with Movable Objects
(CLEAR), learns to select objects and propose alternative
interaction orders from scene observations and robot structure.
For each proposed sequence, it generates object references,
conditioning each prediction on those planned for preceding
interactions. The planner checks whether candidate plans are
feasible in the proposed interaction order, selects the valid
candidate with the fewest object interactions, and replans
from updated observations during execution. Our approach is
evaluated in three simulation environments: 2D grids, ordered
manipulation, and maze navigation. The maze experiments
assess the effect of robot-structure conditioning and the ability
to replan when environmental perturbations block access to
required objects. Code, videos, and results are available at:
https://anonymous.4open.science/w/clear-page-1209/.
I. INTRODUCTION
Robots operating in homes and workplaces perform tasks
in spaces occupied by furniture, equipment, and other ob-
jects. A box can block a corridor, while objects on a table can
occupy the space needed for manipulation. Moving selected
objects can open a path for navigation or free space for
a desired arrangement. However, moving one object can
obstruct a subsequent interaction. Planning these changes
requires considering how object motions affect the space
available for completing the task.
We refer to planning object interactions for navigation
and object arrangement as Planning Among Movable Ob-
jects (PAMO). Prior work has studied how object reloca-
tion enables navigation through clutter [1], [2]. Navigation
tasks specify a destination, while arrangement tasks spec-
ify conditions on the resulting object configurations. Both
tasks require selecting objects, determining the interaction
order, and planning the motion of each selected object.
The resulting plan must allow the robot to complete the
required interactions and achieve the task goal. Because
object relocation requires additional execution effort, we aim
to achieve the goal with the minimum number of object
interactions.
Even with the scene and goal fixed, robots with different
capabilities can require different interaction plans. A robot
capable of crossing a step can bypass a blocked corridor,
whereas another embodiment must move objects to clear an

alternative path. Reach and force limits further determine
which objects can be moved and which motions can be exe-
cuted. Feasibility also changes as preceding interactions alter
the scene. For example, moving a box away from one target
can obstruct the approach to another target or occupy space
needed for a subsequent motion. Stilman and Kuffner [3]
address these dependencies by constraining preceding object
displacements using the requirements of subsequent motions.
Object selection, interaction order, and continuous motion
must therefore be considered together under the capabilities
of the robot.
The same robot can achieve a task goal through different
object selections and interaction orders. Different plans can
achieve the same goal with the same number of object inter-
actions, even when different objects are selected. Alternative
plans provide options when execution errors or scene changes
prevent the initially planned interactions. Generative models
learn distributions over trajectories and action sequences to
represent alternative behaviors [4], [5]. In PAMO, a learned
distribution over interaction plans can represent alternative
object selections, interaction orders, and the corresponding
continuous motions.
To address these challenges, we present Capability-Aware
Latent OrdEring for Adaptive InteRaction with Movable
Objects (CLEAR). The main contribution is an embodiment-
aware generative planner that learns object selection, inter-

a common framework. Predicted interaction feasibility aug-

Among feasible candidates satisfying the task goal, the
planner selects a plan with the minimum number of object
interactions. Updated scene observations guide replanning
of the remaining interactions during execution. We conduct
four experiments across 2D grid, ordered manipulation, and
maze navigation settings to evaluate interaction feasibility,
plan diversity, embodiment conditioning, and recovery under
environmental changes.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Planning Among Movable Objects
In planning among movable objects, relocating an ob-
ject can alter the feasibility of subsequent interactions. For
navigation, object relocation enables robot motion through
clutter, as studied in Navigation Among Movable Obstacles
(NAMO) [1]. Ren et al. [2] introduce PAMO*, a search-
based method for joint navigation and relocation plan-
ning without predefined final object configurations, while
Interactive-FAR [6] updates navigation routes using interac-
tion feedback. In object rearrangement, achieving the target
arrangement may require moving objects to temporary loca-
tions [7]. Stilman and Kuffner [3] constrain object relocations
according to the requirements of subsequent interactions.
ReloPush [8] plans rearrangements under nonholonomic mo-
tion and pushing constraints.
Beyond planning object motion, prior work considers the
physical stability and semantic suitability of resulting object
configurations. SPOTS [9] combines physical stability veri-
fication with semantic reasoning to identify suitable configu-
rations. Our method instead generates alternative interaction
plans conditioned on the scene and robot structure and selects
a feasible plan with the fewest interactions.
B. Generative Models for Robotic Planning
The success of generative models in language and vision
has motivated research on generating diverse robot behaviors.
Diffuser [4] and Diffusion Policy [5] learn distributions over
trajectories and observation-conditioned action sequences,
respectively. SMORE [10] generates diverse manipulation
options for semi-autonomous teleoperation through quality-
diversity sampling and latent-variable policies. Planned ob-
ject motions must satisfy geometric constraints and allow
subsequent interactions. StructDiffusion [11] generates ob-
ject arrangements under language and geometric constraints,
while Diffusion-CCSP [12] combines constraint-specific dif-
fusion models to solve continuous constraints in task and
motion planning. Generative Skill Chaining [13] composes
learned skill distributions to generate long-horizon plans for a
given skill sequence, while Generative Factor Chaining [14]

combines spatial constraints and skill transitions within a
given symbolic plan graph. In contrast, our approach jointly
learns object selection and interaction ordering to generate
alternative plans. Conditional flow matching [15] gener-
ates continuous interaction parameters for each sequence,
conditioned on the full observed scene and the generated
parameters of preceding interactions.
C. Embodiment-Aware Robot Planning
Robots with different structures can require different
control strategies for the same task. NerveNet [16] and
Shared Modular Policies [17] encode robot structure through
message passing between body or actuator representa-
tions. MetaMorph [18], Body Transformer [19], and GET-
Zero [20] incorporate morphology and body connectivity
into Transformer-based control. Beyond controller transfer,
XSkill [21] and shared goal-conditioned policies [22] study
cross-embodiment learning through skill representations and
experience from heterogeneous robots.
At the task level, robot capabilities determine which
actions are feasible in the scene. CLARA [23] combines
descriptions of robot functions and scene context to assess
command feasibility and resolve ambiguity. E2-CARE [24]
adapts reusable skill templates using constraints from robot
embodiment and the environment. Our work uses capability
information to determine the required object interactions for
a fixed scene and goal. We condition scene representations on
robot structure to predict traversal and interaction feasibility
and support object selection and ordering.
III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
A. Embodiment-Aware Planning Among Movable Objects
We focus on the problem of planning object interactions
to achieve navigation or arrangement goals. Let S denote
a scene consisting of the observed environment geometry,
the current robot state, N movable objects {oi}N
i=1, and a
task goal G. Depending on the task, G specifies a nav-
igation destination or a desired object arrangement. Each
object oi = (xi, ai) is described by configuration xi and
physical attributes ai, including geometry and mass. The
robot embodiment B is described by link, joint, and actuator
properties. An interaction plan π = ((i1, ξ1), . . . , (iK, ξK))
is a sequence of K object interactions. The sequence ρ =
(i1, . . . , iK) specifies the selected objects and the interaction
order. For interaction k, we define ξk as the target configu-
ration or trajectory of the selected object, depending on the
task representation.
B. Interaction Feasibility and Planning Objective
Interaction k is feasible if the robot can reach the selected
object and perform the object motion required by ξk while
satisfying the relevant geometric and physical constraints.
Interaction feasibility is evaluated in the scene resulting
from preceding object interactions. A plan π is valid if all
required robot motions and object interactions are feasible
and the final scene satisfies the task goal G. The planning
objective is to find a valid plan with the minimum number
of object interactions. When the task goal G is achievable
without object interaction, the minimum interaction count
is K = 0. We learn a conditional distribution pθ(π | S, B)
over interaction plans, where θ denotes the trainable model
parameters. The planner generates candidate plans from the
learned distribution and selects a valid candidate with the
minimum number of object interactions.
IV. PROPOSED METHOD
Our approach learns the conditional plan distribution
pθ(π | S, B) through embodiment-aware scene grounding, la-
tent interaction ordering, and rank-causal generation (Fig. 2).
Affordance-Guided Encoding forms a planning context H
from scene observations and robot structure (Sec. IV-A).
OrderNet determines object selection and interaction order
(Sec. IV-B), and CausalFlowNet generates continuous inter-
action parameters under the proposed order (Sec. IV-C). A
low-level planner checks candidate feasibility and computes
the required robot motions, with updated observations guid-
ing control and replanning (Sec. IV-D).
A. Embodiment-Aware Scene Grounding
To ground scene representations in robot capabilities,
Affordance-Guided Encoding augments object features with
predicted interaction availability. An embodiment encoder
represents the structural properties of B as an embedding
zB using shared feature encoding and average pooling.
Conditioned on zB and local scene observations, the network
predicts an affordance probability ˆpaff for each candidate
object interaction or terrain transition. A binary target b indi-
cates whether the object interaction is available or the terrain
transition is feasible. The network is trained by minimizing
the binary cross-entropy loss Laff = BCE(ˆpaff, b).
Using the learned predictions, we augment object features
with interaction probabilities and reachability information.
When terrain geometry constrains robot movement, com-
puting object reachability requires evaluating connectivity
across the scene. Therefore, path search uses the predicted
transition probabilities to determine which objects the robot
can reach. The augmented object features are combined
with the embodiment embedding zB and scene observa-
tions to construct the planning context H for OrderNet and
CausalFlowNet.
B. Latent Interaction Ordering
OrderNet learns object selection and interaction order from
the planning context H. For each object, the network predicts
a selection probability qi and a Gaussian latent score distri-
bution with mean µi and standard deviation σi. Bernoulli
sampling based on qi determines the selected object set I,
and Gaussian sampling generates latent scores ui. Sorting the
selected scores from lowest to highest defines the interaction
order [25],

The network is trained to predict the object selections and
interaction orders specified in the training data. The training
objective is
Lorder = Lsel + Lrank + λKLLKL.
(2)
The selection loss Lsel trains object selection using binary
cross-entropy between the predicted probabilities qi and the
object selection labels. The weighted Bradley–Terry loss [26]
Lrank encourages lower scores for preceding objects, with
greater weight on pairs close in the training order. Gaussian
reparameterization enables gradient-based training of the
score parameters. The regularizer LKL penalizes divergence
of the predicted Gaussian distributions from a standard
normal distribution.
C. Rank-Causal Generation
Given the object set I and interaction order ρ obtained in
Sec. IV-B, CausalFlowNet generates continuous interaction
parameters conditioned on H. For each selected object, rank
denotes its position in ρ. We represent object parameters by a
matrix Yt ∈RN×D, where t ∈[0, 1] denotes flow time. Each
row yi(t) contains D coordinates for object oi. The generator
produces target configurations or complete object trajectories
at t = 1 (see Fig. 2(c)). The network predicts a velocity
field vt = vθ(Yt, t | H, ρ) to update these parameters. Rank-
causal attention combines the token for each selected object
with generated tokens from preceding ranks and the context
H. The context is shared because scene and robot infor-
mation is available before generation. The attention mask
blocks generated information from entering context tokens,
preventing subsequent predictions from affecting preceding
predictions indirectly through H.
In the training phase, we use conditional flow match-
ing [15] to train the velocity field. Training data contain
I, ρ, and target object parameters Ytarget. For selected
objects, active coordinates are those requiring prediction,
excluding padding and fixed coordinates. We initialize the
active elements of Y0 with independent noise from N(0, 1)
and sample t ∼U[0, 1]. On the active coordinates, the
interpolated state and flow loss are

The auxiliary loss Lavail penalizes unavailable objects ac-
cording to normalized first-interaction weights proportional
to qi exp(−µi). Training labels determine availability, and

In the inference phase, I, ρ, and H remain fixed through-
out flow integration. Using the same rank-causal attention,
we integrate dYt/dt = vt from Gaussian noise Y0 at t = 0
to generate Y1 at t = 1. The selected rows of Y1 are
decoded in the order ρ into (ξ1, . . . , ξK) to construct the
interaction plan π. For the same I and ρ, different initial
noise values allow the planner to generate alternative target
configurations or object trajectories. The planner checks
candidate plans for feasibility before execution (Sec. IV-D).
D. Execution and Replanning
As shown in Fig. 2(d), candidate plans are checked for
robot reachability, collision avoidance, and interaction con-
straints before execution. Validation follows ρ and considers
the effects of preceding object motions, but is omitted in the
Grid and Ordered Manipulation evaluations. Among feasible
candidates satisfying the task goal G, the planner selects
a plan with the minimum number of object interactions. A
valid plan requiring no object interaction bypasses contin-
uous generation. For legged embodiments, an MPC-based
controller follows a policy-guided control structure [27], with
command optimization adapted from [28]. Candidate com-
mand sequences are evaluated through rollouts of a learned
locomotion policy to perform the planned object interactions.
The optimization retains high-performing and behaviorally
diverse command sequences, following a quality-diversity
principle [10]. We combine this optimization with Carte-
sian tracking and joint-command smoothing (Fig. 3). The
controller executes an initial segment of the best evaluated
command sequence and updates the command optimization
using new state estimates. After each object interaction, up-
dated scene observations guide replanning of the remaining
interactions.

V. EXPERIMENTS
In this section, we evaluate our proposed method across
complementary task settings. The experiments address four
questions. (1) Can the planner identify the required objects
and recover executable minimum-interaction plans, including
alternative optimal sequences? (2) Can the planner complete
manipulation tasks while satisfying interaction precondi-
tions? (3) How do embodiment information and learned
affordances affect planning for different robots in the same
scene? (4) When does closed-loop replanning improve task
completion after environmental changes?
We conduct four experiments in three environments shown
in Fig. 4: 2D Grid, Ordered Manipulation adapted from
OGBench [29], and Maze Navigation. Training data com-
prise exact-search Grid solutions, policy demonstrations for
Ordered Manipulation, and reference sequences and object
trajectories for Maze Navigation. For Maze Navigation,
embodiment-specific control policies are trained and fine-
tuned using mjlab [30] and kept fixed across planning
methods. At inference, the trained planning modules run on
an NPU. Results are averaged across seeds, with ± denoting
the sample standard deviation (i.e., SD) when provided.
A. 2D Grid Task
a) Task and Setup:
The 2D Grid Task evaluates
interaction-order dependence and alternative optimal se-
quences for reaching the goal with the fewest object interac-
tions. Each interaction moves one object to a target cell, and
navigation steps do not contribute to the interaction count.
Scenes contain an agent, static walls, and movable objects
on 16×16, 24×24, or 32×32 grids. We consider five scene
families (Fig. 5). Direct requires no interaction, Single-Gate
requires one, and Chain requires multiple interactions in a
specific order. Branch allows alternative optimal sequences,
while Distractor includes irrelevant objects.
b) Baselines and Evaluation: We compare CLEAR
with three adapted baselines and two ordering variants, all
trained on interaction plans obtained by exact search with
additional training on separate scenes. Autoregressive [31]
selects objects sequentially without repetition and terminates
with a learned STOP token. Gumbel–Sinkhorn [32] jointly
assigns objects to sequence positions and selects objects pre-
ceding STOP. PolyNet [33] generates alternative sequences
by conditioning a shared autoregressive decoder on four
distinct inputs, with supervised training replacing reinforce-
ment learning. For each reference sequence, PolyNet uses the
Fig. 5: 2D Grid scenes: initial states (top) and an optimal
plan per scene (bottom). Red marks goals; green, blue, and
gray denote the agent, movable objects, and walls.
lowest prediction loss across the four inputs. CLEAR-RO
randomly shuffles the predicted interaction order, whereas
CLEAR-HO orders the same selected objects by increasing
initial Manhattan distance.
CLEAR receives indicators of reachable pushing positions
and allowed push directions for each object. For single-plan
evaluation, our planner orders objects by mean predicted
priority and selects the most frequently predicted target cell
across four samples. Execution stops at the first infeasible
interaction. Task success rate (Task S/R) is the percentage
of scenes in which the agent reaches the goal. Minimum-
interaction success rate (Min. S/R) additionally requires
exactly K⋆interactions, the minimum obtained by exact
search. Coverage (Cov.@8) is the percentage of optimal
object sequences recovered among the first eight proposals
per scene, regardless of execution success. Invalid rate
(Inv.@8) measures the execution failure rate among the first
eight proposals per scene.
c) Results and Analysis:
Our planner achieves the
highest mean Task S/R (96.16%) and Min. S/R (96.02%),
indicating that nearly all successful plans use the minimum
number of interactions (Table I). Using random (CLEAR-
RO) or distance-based (CLEAR-HO) interaction orders re-
duces mean Task S/R to 34.12% and 61.76%, respectively.
The ordering ablations highlight the importance of preserving
the planned interaction order. Our planner also achieves the
highest mean Cov.@8 (88.11%) and lowest mean Inv.@8
(6.43%), supporting broader coverage of optimal object
sequences alongside fewer execution failures.
B. Ordered Manipulation Task
a) Task and Setup: We evaluate whether our planner
completes manipulation tasks while satisfying interaction
preconditions. In the adapted OGBench Scene environ-
ment [29], a UR5e arm interacts with a cube, two buttons,
a drawer, and a sliding window. The scene observation
specifies which buttons must be activated before moving the
drawer or window. Placing the cube inside a closed drawer
requires opening it, inserting the cube at a target determined
by the drawer’s intermediate position, and closing it. We train
on seven combinations of button requirements and evaluate
on two unseen combinations.
b) Baselines and Evaluation: We compare our planner
with three baselines and two separately trained ablations.

All methods share an MPC-based controller and replan
after each interaction, with up to 12 attempts including
retries. After three consecutive failures at the same target
with little change in object states, an alternative target is
tried if available. Task success rate (Task S/R) measures
the percentage of episodes with correct button states and

respective goals. Valid success rate (Valid S/R) additionally
requires every attempted interaction to satisfy interaction
preconditions. Invalid episode rate (Invalid E/R) measures
the percentage of episodes with at least one interaction
attempted with unmet preconditions.
c) Results and Analysis: CLEAR achieves the highest
mean Task S/R (92.17%) and Valid S/R (91.92%), with a gap
of 0.25 percentage points between the two metrics (Table II).
Classical Search and BC-Grounding achieve lower Invalid
E/R (0.83% and 0.67%, respectively), although both methods
achieve lower Valid S/R than CLEAR. Removing affordance-
related components reduces Task S/R by 2.50 and Valid S/R
by 6.59 percentage points, while increasing Invalid E/R from
1.28% to 7.75%. The affordance ablation supports the role
of conditioning and supervision in selecting interactions with
satisfied preconditions. Removing the rank mask results in a
smaller decrease in Valid S/R, from 91.92% to 90.33%, and
increases Invalid E/R from 1.28% to 3.08%.

b) Baselines and Evaluation: We compare our plan-
ner with adapted NAMO-LLM1 [36] and CDGS [37],
which learns object-interaction transitions using our per-
ception and terrain assessment components. NAMO-LLM
(w/o LLM) uniformly samples objects passing geometric
checks. CLEAR-Specialists trains one planner per embodi-
ment under the same combined training budget as our shared
model. CLEAR-Robot-ID and CLEAR + GET replace our
structural encoder with a learned robot-identity embedding
and an adapted Graph Embodiment Transformer [20], respec-
tively. CLEAR-No-Embodiment removes embodiment and
capability-conditioned navigation features, while CLEAR-
No-Affordance replaces learned terrain guidance with geo-
metric checks, retaining affordance supervision.
All methods use the same controller per embodiment and
allow up to eight candidate plans and two object interactions
without high-level replanning. Success rate (S/R) measures
the percentage of episodes completing the task with final
position changes below 0.20 m for objects not targeted by
interaction attempts. Planning accuracy (P/A) measures the
percentage of cases where the planner produces a valid goal-
reaching plan or correctly identifies the task as infeasible for
the robot. We evaluate S/R for G1, Spot, and Spot+Arm, and
P/A for Husky, with 45 Standard and 30 High-Mass trials per
method and embodiment across three seeds.
c) Results and Analysis: Our planner achieves higher
mean scores than the adapted external planners across all
evaluated settings (Table III). The shared model achieves
the highest Spot+Arm S/R in Standard (95.6%) and High-
Mass (96.7%), and exceeds CLEAR-Specialists on High-
Mass G1 (93.3% versus 73.3%), although Specialists per-
form best in several other comparisons. Our planner also
exceeds CLEAR-Robot-ID and CLEAR + GET for Spot,
Spot+Arm, and Husky in both sets, but not for G1. Re-
moving embodiment information reduces High-Mass G1
S/R from 93.3% to 6.7% and Husky P/A from 100.0%
to 10.0%. On Standard, CLEAR-No-Affordance achieves
60.0% Spot+Arm S/R compared with 95.6% for our planner,
supporting the benefit of learned terrain guidance over geo-

D. Long-Horizon Replanning
a) Task and Setup: This experiment evaluates recovery
from environmental changes during long-horizon execution.
We evaluate G1 in 12 MuJoCo scenes with six-interaction
reference plans under three conditions: Nominal, Place-
ment, and Access. In Nominal, execution proceeds without
disturbance. In Placement, a manipulated object is moved
away from the target position. In Access, another object is
relocated to alter access to subsequent interactions.
b) Baseline and Evaluation: We compare CLEAR-
No-Replanning and CLEAR using the same checkpoint,
controller, low-level feedback, and execution limits. Both
allow up to 14 interaction attempts, retrying failures once
along the same object’s remaining planned path. CLEAR-
No-Replanning follows the initial plan and stops after a
failed retry, while CLEAR replans after successful interac-
tions or failed retries. If replanning finds no valid candidate,
the remaining plan is executed when available (i.e., residual
fallback). Planning allows 15 calls, 300 s total wall-clock
time, and 60 s per call. Success requires task completion
without prohibited contact or wall penetration, with unin-
tended object position changes below 0.10 m, excluding the
external disturbance.

c) Results and Analysis: CLEAR achieves higher mean
S/R in all three conditions (Table IV). The improvement
is largest in the Access scenario with S/R increasing from
50.0% to 91.7%. S/R increases by 5.6 and 5.3 percentage
points in the Nominal and Placement scenarios, respectively.
These results support updating the remaining plan when envi-
ronmental changes alter object placement or the reachability
of subsequent interaction locations.
VI. CONCLUSION
We present CLEAR, a capability-aware approach to plan-
ning coupled object selection, interaction order, and ob-
ject motion. Affordance-guided scene grounding connects
these decisions to robot capabilities, while latent ordering
represents alternative sequences and rank-causal generation
conditions object motions on preceding interactions. The
experiments demonstrate executable minimum-interaction
planning in grids, closed-loop manipulation under changing
preconditions, and capability-conditioned navigation with a
shared planning model. The long-horizon evaluation demon-
strates recovery when environmental changes invalidate the
remaining plan. Future work will extend sequence-dependent
object-motion generation beyond the current interaction rep-
resentations and validate the plans on physical robots.
